CONVENTION PLANS COMPLETED
Brother Rod TiUman, Rho '56, reports that
plans for the 122nd Anniversary Convention
of Psi Upsilon are near
completion and that
all is in readiness for the descent of Psi U's
upon the Four Lakes City of Madison, Wis
consin.
September promises to be its usual en
chanting self on the Wisconsin campus, and
Brothers should come
prepared to enjoy the
"Vacation Convention" on the shores of Lake
Mendota. An early morning dip from the
Psi U pier is part of the ritual, as is the
sight of the "glorious orb of day" setting beyond Picnic Point.
From the first breakfast at the Chapter House on
Wednesday morning to the last pretzel
at Picnic Point on
Saturday, the 1955 Convention promises to be one that all of those
present will forever treasure in their memories.
The Rho asks that Brothers one and all accept our invitation and plan to be with us to
renew fraternal spirit once more.

Alan Gerald Gowman, Theta '50
A
BLINDED soldier who "didn't want
to be put outside the game of life"
received his Ph.D. degree from Harvard
University on
Thursday, June 16, 1955.
Brother Alan Gerald Gowman, 30, of
Chappaqua, New York, was blinded near
Anzio in May 1944, but now is ready to
carve out a career as a teacher of sociology
at college.
And his massive doctoral thesis shows
how American society unwittingly rele
gates blind men to a
subserviency they
neither want nor deserve.
"When I was bhnded," Gowman says,
"I decided to ask no
quarter from anyone.
"I decided to conform to the same rules
as
everybody else. Sob stuff wasn't the
way I wanted it. I wanted to hve on the
same terms met by others in society.
"I didn't want to be put outside the
game of life."
And for Gowman, achieving a doctorate
means, among other things, that he is hold
ing his own in competition with sighted
persons. It means that he is proving him
self by the ground rules he has laid down
for his hfe.
Brother Gowman was inducted into the
Army in July 1943. Only a month earlier,
he graduated from Horace Greeley High
School, where he says he was interested
only in "blondes, football, and Model-A
cars." He had failed a course, gotten C's
and D's in others and played end on the
football team. He was
"very casual about
the academic world."
Less than a
year later, as a
19-year-old
rifleman with the 36th Division I43rd
Infantry, at VeHtri near Anzio, Gowman
was wounded in both eyes, and the doctors
took them out. In July 1946, after exten
sive plastic surgery and rehabilitation at
Valley Forge Hospital and at Avon Old
Farms, Connecticut, the Army discharged
him.
Civihan life brought disappointment.
While he was in the hospital he was treated
as a man like other men, bhnd or
sighted,
whole or maimed. Outside, he says, people
sympathized too much.
Sometime earlier, he had decided not to
change his old ways of getting along with
other people and not to change the ways
he looked at himself. He did not want to
live his life under different rules from his
neighbors.
So, when he was
finally discharged, he
decided that "it was
important to
go to
college."
"That," he says, "would be the initial
barrier to face�the initial step in compet
ing with sighted people." He felt he had
to start proving himself by the rules he had
laid down for himself.
Brother Gowman, having entered in
1946, graduated from Union College with
a B.A. degree in three years. He made Phi
Beta Kappa, received the Archibald Award
for scholarship in English Literature, and
served on the student council and inter
fraternity council. He majored in English
and minored in sociology. In the fall of
1949, he entered Harvard as a Ph.D. canAlan Gerald Gowman, Theta '50

didate in Social Relations. He received
his M.A. in 1951.
He has his own two-room apartment
in Cambridge and gets around the univer
sity pretty much on his own. Until 1953,
the Veterans Administration paid most
of his expenses under the G.I. Bill, but
since that time he has made his own
wayfirst winning a Social Science Research
Council Fellowship in 1953 and then se
curing a
position as a tutor under Harv
ard's undergraduate tutorial program. He
was consultant to the Veterans Administra
tion on a
documentary film concerning
blindness.
The most tangible yield of his six years
at Harvard is a thick volume entitled "The
War Blind In American Social Structure."
This doctoral thesis examines the way
American society regards the blind and
the way the blind regard themselves. It
reveals that a blind man isn't the same
person that most of us think he is.
Brother Gowman first questioned high
school students to discover what exactly
was the common American attitude toward
the blind. He discovered there is a stereo
type. People regard all blind men as de
pendent, as
people who can't function ade
quately and who need to be supported and
coddled. And if any blind man does any
thing outstanding, the common belief is
that he's a
genius.
Next, Gowman questioned 14 selected
blinded veterans to fix the picture they had
of themselves. He found that they don't
define themselves as
inadequate or
incapa
ble of functioning. Many resent being
coddled, and want to achieve the same
goals that sighted persons pursue. Those
that do achieve outstanding things don't
see themselves as
geniuses at all. Their
achievements stem from the same roots
as the achievements of sighted persons;
abihty and hard work. Some, of course,
were weak before being blinded, and so
they accept the dependent role that so
ciety gives them. But the "active blind"�
Gowman says he's one of these�run
against the tide. They try to get outside
of the stereotyped role pressed on them
by society.
And so, Gowman discovered a
gap be
tween what we think a blind man is and
what a blind man thinks he is.
"Certainly," Brother Gowman says,
"blindness causes certain intrinsic losses.
But many bhnd men learn to live with
them, and they desire, to the greatest ex
tent possible, to be regarded as
having
an
individuality, a
uniqueness and a set
of ambitions just hke anyone else. The big
trouble, however, is that people have a
way of generalizing the specific handicap
of the blind man.
People think that a bhnd
man is also without a whole range of hu
man
potentiality. They think he's not only
less than a man, but less even than a bhnd
man. The press of this way of thinking
prevents a blind man from developing his
personality to the full. It impoverishes him,
and, whether he likes it or not, it tends to
force him into a role of subserviency."
Brother Gowman also studied a kind of
person he calls "companion to the bhnd."
These are the people who treat a blind
man
just as
they treat others, giving no
more and no less, and expecting no more
and no less. They would sympathize if
the blind were affronted, but they also
would tell a blind man to "shape up" if
he started acting like a child.
"Companions to the blind are not neces
sarily people who live or work with the
blind. They're people," says Gowman,
"who have the capacity to understand the
way a blind man
regards himself, and to
act accordingly."
Brother Cowman's thesis is a scientific
work in sociology. It doesn't preach and
isn't meant to. It simply brings to light
facts and inter-relationships that hitherto
have not been thoroughly investigated.
The American Foundation for the Blind is
planning to consider the work for publica
tion.
To prepare the thesis, Gowman em
ployed "readers"�college students who
came to his apartment and both read to
him and took dictation. For, almost none
of the books he had read either in courses
or in preparing the thesis have been ren
dered in Braille. The Veterans Administra
tion paid the readers while Gowman was
ehgible; for two years he has been paying
them himself.

By Robert T. McCracken, Tau '04
OWEN JOSEPHUS ROBERTS, an out
standing member of Psi Upsilon, was
born in Germantown, a suburb of Phila
delphia, on
May 2, 1875. His paternal
grandfather, William Owen Roberts, came
to this country from Wales in 1808. His
maternal grandmother was a descendant of
early German settlers in Pennsylvania.
There were, accordingly, fused in him the
fighting qualities and forensic skill of the
Celt and the painstaking industry and pas
sion for accuracy of the Teuton. Through
out his life he exemplified these character
istics.
He was educated at the Germantown
Academy, a school founded in 1760, and
at the University of Pennsylvania, from
which he received his Bachelor of Arts
Degree in 1895 and his Bachelor of Law
Degree in 1898. He was elected to Psi
Upsilon and to Phi Beta Kappa while in
College and was
graduated from The Law
School with the highest honors. Immedi
ately upon graduation, he became associ
ated with The Law School as an instruc
tor, and later became an assistant professor
and eventually a full professor, conducting
courses there until 1917. His interest in
the School continued throughout his life.
so much so that after retiring from the
Supreme Court, he accepted an invitation
in 1948 to serve as its Dean, on a
tempo
rary basis and without compensation, and
continued such service for three years.
Justice Roberts early obtained recogni
tion as a court
lawyer of the first magni
tude. In 1903 he was named First Assist
ant District Attorney of Philadelphia and
served in that position until 1906. In 1912
he formed a
partnership with WiUiam W.
Montgomery, Jr. and Charles L. McKeehan, the latter of whom became a
Judge
of the United States District Court for the
Eastern District of Pennsylvania. He re
mained a member of this firm until his
elevation to the Bench in 1930. In May of
1918 he was named by the United States
Attorney General as
Special Assistant to
prosecute cases
arising under the World
War I Espionage Act in the Eastern Dis
trict of Pennsylvania. He obtained several
convictions for sedition while serving in
such capacity.
In the years immediately following the
First World War, his practice grew with
unusual rapidity, and he was seen in the
courts, not only of Philadelphia, but in
adjoining counties and states, almost conizes that however hard he tries to be like
everybody else, the blind man
always runs
into some situations in which he has to
have help�traveling, reading and so on.
He has accepted that irreducible mini
mum of handicap, and he says other blind
men
accept it, too. What he and other
"active blind" suffer is society's unwitting
expansion of the handicap to a
point where
blind men are
kept down. He refuses to be
kept down.
Teaching sociology is his ambition. He
got a taste of it this year as a tutor to a
group of Harvard students. At the begin
ning, his students regarded him as the
stereotyped blind man, but .as the year
went on, they discovered their course was
just as hard as others, and just as inter
esting. After a while, they were
calling
up their blind tutor with questions, or ask
ing him out for coffee. "Most," Gowman
says, "found it a
very rewarding year."
Although Gowman knows he wants to
teach, he isn't going into this field at
Harvard. He plans to continue research in
the area of blindness.
"Deprivation," say Gowman, "is rela
tive. As a blinded individual, you try to
work out your life in terms of the limita
tion. You just channel your energies in
new
ways."
Brother Gowman is the son of Mr. and
Mrs. Owen L. Gowman of Orchard Ridge
Rd., Chappaqua, New York.

tinually. During that period he also ac
cepted appointments as director of a num
ber of widely known corporations.
He first attained national prominence
when, on
February 16, 1924, President
Coolidge appointed him as
Special Coun
sel, to serve with former Senator Atlee
Pomerene, to investigate and prosecute the
Tea Pot Dome and Elk Hills Oil cases.
Six years were
spent by the two counsel
in this htigation, resulting in a restoration
to the Navy of all the lands which had
been leased, and later in the conviction of
Secretary of the Interior Albert B. Fall,
and the holding in senatorial and judicial
contempt of Harry F. Sinclair. These ac
complishments called him so
prominently
to the attention of the Nation that when,
on
May 9, 1930, President Hoover ap
pointed him an Associate Justice of the
Supreme Court of the United States, his
nomination was almost immediately unani
mously confirmed by the Senate. He took
his place on the Bench on
June 2, 1930,
and retained it until his resignation fifteen
years later on
July 5, 1945.
Almost immediately after his assump
tion of his judicial duties, the Court found
itseff presented with problems of the most
vexing nature, arising out of legislation
enacted in an effort to relieve the country
of the effects of the Great Depression, and
later as a result of the New Deal. The
Court was
evenly divided when Justice
Roberts took his seat, between the socalled Conservatives and Liberals. It was,
accordingly, widely beheved and re
peatedly stated that Justice Roberts for a
number of years held the balance of
power, and that the way he voted deter
mined the issue. The justification for this
belief lay in his independence of thought
and his approach to the constitutional
questions involved in the many appeals
which came before the Court in those
days. His concept of the judicial function,
in its approach to a solution of a consti
tutional question, was, as he often said, to
lay the statute down beside the Consti
tution and see whether there was
any
article or section of the latter with which
the statute came into confhct. If he could
find none, he voted to sustain. If he could
find any sufficiently serious, he voted to
strike down the act. Accordingly, he was
often branded as a Conservative and again
as a Liberal. But he was neither. He did
not believe that a
judge's social or
pohtical
philosophy should tinge, much less con
trol, his judicial determination of a con
stitutional question. He was often criti
cized by those who did not agree with his
conclusions, but this is the penalty of in
dependence of thought. In his later years
on the Bench, he found himself frequently
in disagreement with the majority, and,
wherever he deemed it of value to the
clarification of the law, he wrote a dissent
ing opinion. Some of these dissents are
among the most powerful of his contribu
tions.
His one
outstanding service, aside from
his judicial work, while on the Court, was
his acceptance of an
appointment by Presi
dent Roosevelt to head a five man com
mission to fix responsibility for the unpreparedness for the attack on Pearl Harbor.
The report of the commission, prepared by
Justice Roberts but with the invaluable as
sistance of his four colleagues, all of whom
were ofiicers high in the Army, Navy and
Air Force, while the subject of criticism
by those who did not comprehend the
scope of the inquiry, nevertheless is said
to have been instrumental in the Con
gressional demand for the unification of
the services into the Department of De
fense.
Justice Roberts retired from the Bench
at the age of seventy. He did not resume
the active practice of law. He declined to
resume court work, which had been his
chief metier prior to his elevation to the
Bench, coming out of retirement only once,
in December, 1954, to
argue a case in
volving the propriety of a certain action
of the Supreme Court of Pennsylvania. His
interests during the last decade of his life
were, however, many and various. In
tensely interested in the program of a
federation of the Western Democracies,
an interest which began before his retire
ment, he spent much time speaking in
various parts of the country in its behalf,
and later became President of the Atlantic
Union, an
organization devoted to this
project.
In 1946 President Truman called upon

him to head an
amnesty board to review
the cases of some 11,000 persons convicted
of World War II draft violations, and he
also served as chairman of a
special ad
visory board set up to review the cases of
27,500 service personnel convicted by
courts martial during the War.
A leading layman of the Protestant
Episcopal Church, Justice Roberts, in
1946, became one of the first laymen ever
elected as President of the House of
Deputies of the General Convention of
that Church, held in Philadelphia in the
Autumn of that year. During that same
year, he served as Chairman of the Na
tional Mental Health Foundation, and as
Chairman of the National Security Com
mission to advocate universal military
training. In 1952 he was elected President
of the American Philosophical Society, of
which he had long been a member, and
was re-elected in 1953 and 1954.
In 1953 he was elected Chairman of
the Board of the Fund for the Advance
ment of Education, estabhshed by the
Ford Foundation, and in that same
year he
became a member of the Board of Regents
of the Smithsonian Institution at Wash
ington. In his work for the Ford Founda
tion, he traveled extensively, spending sev
eral weeks in the Virgin Islands in 1953
and in Cahfornia in 1954. Elected a
Trustee of the University of Pennsylvania,
his Ahna Mater, while he was still on the
Bench, he took an active part in the de
liberations of that body after his retire
ment and in 1954 headed a committee
appointed to conduct a
survey of all of the
activities of the institution.
Justice Roberts was awarded Honorary
Degrees of Doctor of Laws by a number of
colleges and universities, including the
University of Pennsylvania, and in 1951
he was awarded the Degree of Doctor of
Civil Laws by Oxford University. His in
terest in the field of education never
dwindled, and the degrees so awarded
were a
fitting recognition not only of his
public services but of that interest.
His death, on
May 17, a few days after
his 80th birthday, ended one of the out
standing careers of Americans of our time.
As the New York Herald Tribune so well
put it in its editorial following his decease:
"The possession by any nation of men
of Justice Roberts' independent stripe,
whose sound judgment is instinctively
trusted, is an invaluable asset. To such
as he, when a
supreme controversy rages,
men can look with confidence for an un
biased appraisal of the facts. . . . He died
yesterday after a full life, a man whose
efforts had won him great success and
whose qualities had won the universal
respect of his fellow countrymen."

cago in 1888. Previously, he had attended

quent speaker at fraternity dinners in vari
ous

member of the Executive Council for more
than twenty years.

in the early days of this organization�
from 1900-1921. He founded and served

Syndicate and the Cosmos Broadcasting
Company. He was an outstanding advo
cate of international good will and trade
and made many trips to Japan in various
capacities. He drafted the platform of the
League to Enforce Peace in 1915 and was
a member of the Committee for Reciprocal
World Trade and the International Foreign
Trade Council. Brother Houston was Far
East Commissioner for the New York
World's Fair and helped organize the Ad
vertising Clubs of the World. He was one
of the organizers of the United States
Chamber of Commerce and the Interna
tional Chamber of Commerce.
Brother Houston never hesitated to fight
for issues that he felt were worthwhile. In
1934 he joined the campaign of the Mo
tion Picture Research Council to fight in
decent pictures. He became Chairman of
the Institute for the Advancement of
Visual Education and Vocational Training
and was Vice President of the American
Plan for Medical and Surgical Care. In
1947 he was named Director of the VetHerbert Sherman Houston, Omega '88
erans of Foreign Wars Edition of The Pic
torial History of World War II. He was
author of and published in 1913 a book
entitled Blocking New Wars.

lived at the Columbia Club and was a fre
quent caller at the Psi Upsilon head
quarters. Until his death, he continued ac
tive in all Psi U interests.

winner of the freshman tennis tournament,

ineligibility.

nis career at Milwaukee Country Day by

ond in the freshman tournament behind Nat

William H. Sanborn, Kappa '10
Wilham H. Sanbom, Kappa, '10, died on
June 1, 1955, in Gray, Maine, after a
long
illness. He was 68 years old.
Brother Sanborn was educated at Port
land High School, Bowdoin College, Harvard
University Law School and the Sorbonne,
Paris. He had been trial justice at Gray since
1942 and conducted a law practice there.
His early career was in Portland, where he
was chairman of the Board of Aldermen and
a member of the Common Council prior to the
first World War. He was first an
army officer
in the 78th Division and later in army aviation
during that war. It was after the war that he
remained abroad to study economics at the
Sorbonne.
Returning to this country, he resumed his
law practice and became active in civic affairs
once more. He was chairman of the Police
Examining Board ( 1920-23), a member of the
Civil Traffic Commission (1924-25), and a
onetime secretary of the Maine PubUcity
Bureau.
Brother Sanborn served at one time on the
staff of the Governor of Maine, and was a
past commander of the Harold T. Andrews
Post, American Legion. He was a Member
of the old Porriand Athletic Club, the Port
land Club, Elks, Lincoln Club and Masons.
Surviving is his brother, Oliver T. Sanborn,
Kappa '11, retired Portland fire chief.

Edward Henry Harriman Simmons,
Lambda '98
Edward Henry Harriman Simmons, Lambda
'98, former president of the New York Stock
Exchange, died recently at his New York
home at the age of 78.
Born in Jersey City, Brother Simmons at
tended Stevens School in Hoboken, and Drisler School, New York City, and was
graduated
from Columbia University in 1898.
In 1900 Brother Simmons purchased a seat
on the Exchange and thereafter was for many
years a
partner in the brokerage firm of Butter
and Gross. He became a
governor of the Stock
Exchange in 1909 and was
vice-president from
1921 to 1924. In the latter year he was elected
president, and he retained that office until
1930. He was elected to his earlier post of
vice-president in 1935-36. For nearly thirty
years he served continuously on the governing
committee, in addition to holding places on
various other important committees. At the
outbreak of World War I, he was a member
of the Clearing House Committee.
Among the clubs of which Brother Simmons
was a
present or former member were the
Union, Racquet and Tennis, Links, National
Golf, Pipin Rock and Church.
He was twice married and twice widowed.
Surviving are two daughters of his first mar
riage, two sisters, six grandchildren and one
great-grandchild.
